subject: literature
title: High modernism (c. 1910–30): the sentence comes apart
dek: Woolf, Joyce, Eliot — and, in the same years, 新青年 and Lu Xun, not as a required Asian peer.

thumb.alt: Profile portrait of Virginia Woolf by George Charles Beresford, 1902.

hero.alt: Pink-red cover of the magazine Blast with the title in huge diagonal black letters, 1914.
hero.caption: Blast, no. 1, 1914, edited by Wyndham Lewis. The type is the manifesto: a London magazine trying to look as loud as the century it wanted. High modernism is not only interior monologue. It is also this kind of shouting.

honesty: “High modernism” is a later classroom name for a cluster of European and American experiments with form, especially in the 1910s–20s. The people in this capsule did not agree they were in a school. This capsule looks out from London, Paris, and Dublin — the usual triangle — and then notices that 1918 in Shanghai is the same year, not a sidebar assigned to make the triangle look global.

timeline.label: Blast
timeline.detail: Vorticist magazine, London. Then the war that the type had been rehearsing.

timeline.label: Portrait
timeline.detail: Joyce’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man appears in book form.

timeline.detail: Lu Xun’s “A Madman’s Diary” in New Youth, vol. 4, no. 5. Vernacular Chinese as a literary event.

timeline.label: May Fourth
timeline.detail: Beijing protests; a political date that literary history also has to hold.

timeline.label: Ulysses / Waste Land
timeline.detail: Joyce in Paris (Shakespeare and Company); Eliot in London. A year the syllabus never lets go.

timeline.label: Woolf
timeline.detail: Mrs Dalloway; To the Lighthouse. The day, the house, the mind as structure.

watch.title: T. S. Eliot reads The Waste Land (recording)
watch.note: The text is 1922. Recordings circulate legally via libraries and the Poetry Foundation’s page; this is not a film of 1922.

listen.title: James Joyce reads from Finnegans Wake (Anna Livia Plurabelle)
listen.note: Internet Archive copy of Joyce’s own recording. Later than Ulysses; still his voice.

glossary.explain: Later critical name for early-twentieth-century formal experiment — fragmentation, interiority, mythic scaffolding — especially in English-language literature around 1910–30. The writers did not vote for the label.

A way of writing a mind in motion: associations, sensory fragments, not always a tidy paragraph. Woolf and Joyce are the usual English-language exhibits. The phrase is a critic’s tool, not a 1922 brand name.
Joyce’s 1922 novel, published in Paris by Shakespeare and Company. One day in Dublin (16 June 1904), a Homeric scaffolding, and a censorship history in the English-speaking world.
Eliot’s 1922 poem. Fragments, quotations, notes. Ezra Pound cut it. The notes are part of the poem’s public life, not a teacher’s appendix only.
Woolf’s 1925 novel. A day in London, a party, a war still in the body of a man who was in it. Time is the structure.
Short-lived Vorticist magazine, London, 1914–15, edited by Wyndham Lewis, with Pound among the contributors. Two issues. The cover is a manifesto in type.

Chinese magazine, founded 1915 by Chen Duxiu (first as 青年雜誌 / Youth Magazine). The May 1918 issue printed Lu Xun’s “A Madman’s Diary.” It argued for vernacular writing and a new culture in the same years Europe was calling itself modern.

4 May 1919: student protests in Beijing against the Versailles settlement’s handling of Shandong. “May Fourth” also names a wider New Culture moment — language, gender, science, the nation — that is not a footnote to London.
Lu Xun story, 1918, written in vernacular Chinese. A reader who sees cannibalism in the classical tradition. It is a modernist event in a different language politics.
Sylvia Beach’s Paris bookshop. It published Ulysses in 1922 when British and American houses would not. A shop can be a press.
Loose London circle (Woolfs, Bells, Keynes, Strachey, and others). Useful as an address. Fatal as a synonym for all of modernism.
London avant-garde around Lewis and Blast, briefly, just before and into the First World War. A British answer to Futurism that did not last as a movement and left a very loud magazine.

Written Chinese closer to speech, as opposed to classical literary Chinese. The New Culture argument was that literature had to change language, not only subject. Lu Xun’s 1918 story is a landmark in that change.

fun_fact.title: The Waste Land came with homework
fun_fact.text: When Eliot published The Waste Land in book form in 1922, he added notes. Some explain quotations; some are jokes; some have been treated as a key to a locked poem. He later said the notes began as a way to pad a slim book. Whether you believe the shrug or not, the notes are part of how the poem was sold and taught. A modernist fragment can arrive with its own apparatus.

sections.title: A sentence that still believed in sequence

blocks.text: The novel and the poem, in the late nineteenth century, could still pretend that time was a corridor. Even when they doubted it, they usually walked you through. The decade before 1914 was already restless — free verse, impressionism, a city speeding up — but the war is the fact that later readers use to explain why the corridor broke. It is not the only fact. Cities, psychoanalysis, new print, and a reading public that included more women and more students were already in the room.

blocks.alt: Virginia Woolf in profile, 1902, photograph by George Charles Beresford.
blocks.caption: Virginia Stephen, photographed by George Charles Beresford in 1902 — years before Mrs Dalloway. The public-domain portrait is of a young woman who had not yet written the books this capsule is about. That is useful. Modernism did not arrive fully formed in a 1922 jacket.
blocks.credit: George Charles Beresford / National Portrait Gallery via Wikimedia Commons / public domain

sections.title: 1922 is a year. 1918 is also a year.

blocks.text: From London and Paris the syllabus bunches around 1922: Ulysses from Sylvia Beach’s shop; The Waste Land in The Criterion and then as a book, cut by Pound. Woolf’s major novels come a few years later, but the method is the same family — a day, a mind, a city, a refusal to narrate as if a life were a plot summary.

blocks.alt: Sepia portrait of James Joyce with glasses and a goatee, around 1918.
blocks.caption: James Joyce, photographed by C. P. Curran in 1918, while Ulysses was still appearing in parts and still unfinished. The book would be a 1922 Paris object. The face is already the one the century kept.
blocks.credit: C. P. Curran / Wikimedia Commons / public domain

blocks.alt: T. S. Eliot as a young man in a study, holding a pipe.
blocks.caption: T. S. Eliot, a young man in a study — the usual furniture of the poet as intellectual. The Waste Land (1922) is not a study poem only. It is a collage of other people’s lines, a London of the war’s aftermath, and a set of notes that became part of the work’s public life.

blocks.text: The same years, not as a required pairing: in Shanghai, 新青年 (New Youth / La Jeunesse) was arguing that Chinese literature had to change its language. The May 1918 issue printed Lu Xun’s 「狂人日記」. In 1919, May Fourth made the argument a street. This is not “the Asian Woolf.” It is a contemporaneous fight about vernacular, the nation, and who a written sentence is for — happening while Eliot was assembling fragments and Joyce was finishing a day in Dublin.

blocks.alt: Cover of New Youth magazine, volume 4 number 5, May 1918, listing 狂人日記 by 魯迅.
blocks.caption: 新青年 4:5, May 1918. The contents list includes 魯迅’s 「狂人日記」. The French title La Jeunesse is on the cover. A Shanghai magazine, in the same decade as Blast and Ulysses, announcing that the language of literature would have to change.

blocks.alt: Studio portrait of Lu Xun in a light changshan, dated Shanghai, 24 September 1930.
blocks.caption: Lu Xun, Shanghai, 24 September 1930, inscribed at age fifty. The photograph is later than “A Madman’s Diary.” It is the face that the 1918 story, and the years after May Fourth, made public.

blocks.text: Blast, in 1914, is the London version of shouting. Two issues, then a war that killed some of the people who might have kept shouting. High modernism is often taught as interior whisper. The pink cover is a reminder that it also wanted to be a poster.

sections.title: Four writers, one decade, not one school

people.name: Virginia Woolf
people.caption: Beresford, 1902.
people.text: Mrs Dalloway (1925), To the Lighthouse (1927), A Room of One’s Own (1929). The sentence as a record of attention. Bloomsbury is the address, not the whole explanation.

people.name: James Joyce
people.caption: Curran, 1918.
people.text: Dublin on the page, published in Paris when London and New York were still afraid of the book. Ulysses is a day and a trial and a shop.

people.name: T. S. Eliot
people.alt: T. S. Eliot as a young man.
people.caption: A study portrait, early career.
people.text: American-born, London-settled. The Waste Land is the poem the century assigned to 1922. The notes, the quotations, and Pound’s cuts are part of the object.

people.name: Lu Xun 魯迅
people.caption: Shanghai, 1930.
people.text: Zhou Shuren. “A Madman’s Diary,” then a body of stories, essays, and translations that made vernacular literary Chinese a fact. He is in this capsule because 1918 is 1918 — not because a Western syllabus needed an Asian twin.

sections.title: A magazine cover is also a sentence

blocks.caption: Blast 1, 1914. The word is the picture.

blocks.text: Put Blast next to 新青年. One is a London roar in English, two issues, a war. The other is a Shanghai magazine that ran for years and printed a story that helped change the written language. They are not the same project. They share a decade in which people decided the old sentence was part of the problem. That is enough of a reason to put them in one capsule. It is not a reason to make one the key to the other.

sections.title: The syllabus, and what it leaves in the corridor

blocks.text: By the 1930s the experiments had become a canon in some places and a target in others. Woolf died in 1941; Joyce the same year; Lu Xun in 1936; Eliot lived to be a monument. The after of high modernism is partly a teaching machine: 1922 as a fetish year, stream of consciousness as a worksheet. The after is also every later writer who inherited the broken corridor and had to decide whether to mend it.
If this archive later takes a Thursday to a different literature, it will not be to complete a set. It will be because another year also happened.
When a syllabus says “1922,” whose 1918 was dropped to make the year look clean?
